prompt.context: Our client is Down Under Apparel, an Australian-based swimwear and lifestyle company. The company unexpectedly missed its internal earnings target. The CEO has called Deloitte to diagnose the problem.
prompt.question: Why did Down Under Apparel miss its earnings forecast, and what should the company do about it?

clarifying_info.a: Competitors vary by product. Historically, Maui was the largest rival in surf and athletic swimwear, offering lower quality products at lower price points. The client has no interest in growth through competitor acquisition.

Two main segments: Surfers and Professional Athletes (30% of revenue) who value performance and cutting-edge hydrodynamic technology, willing to pay for performance but income-constrained; and Luxury Seekers (70% of revenue), the fastest-growing segment, casual users who value the brand and aesthetics.

clarifying_info.q: What channels does Down Under sell through?
clarifying_info.a: Four channels: Surf Shops (small independent retailers in beach towns, mostly performance wear, long-standing relationships); Big Box Retailers (like Dick's, price-sensitive customers, wide variety of performance wear, frequent sales); Department Stores (like Bloomingdale's, least price-sensitive, focus on lifestyle and resort collection); Direct to Consumer Online (repeat customers familiar with the brand, never puts anything on sale).

exhibits.title: Financial Trends
exhibits.shows: Two bar charts side by side: Sales by Year (Forecast vs. Actual, 2012-2014) and Costs by Year (Forecast vs. Actuals, 2012-2014). Note: in millions ($).

exhibits.title: Forecast Details
exhibits.shows: Two tables: 2014 Sales Forecast by Channel and Category ($MM) and 2014 Projected Units Sold by Channel and Category. Channels: Big Box, Department, Online, Surf Shops. Categories: Beach Attire, Casual Swim, Professional Swim, Resort Wear, Surf Equipment.

exhibits.title: Sales by Category (Actuals)
exhibits.shows: A grouped bar chart of Net Sales by Category for 2012, 2013, and 2014 (Casual Swim, Professional Swim, Resort Wear, Beach Attire, Surf Equipment). A table of Average Price by Category (2014). A bar chart of Margin by Category. Note: in millions ($).

exhibits.title: Cost Information (Actuals)
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart of Average Cost by Category broken down by Materials, Labor, Marketing, Shipping, and SG&A for each category (Casual Swim, Professional Swim, Surf Equipment, Beach Attire, Resort Wear). Accompanied by Other Information bullet points.

other_info: Down Under offers free shipping for Direct to Consumer sales due to competitive pressures
Down Under is opening a new manufacturing and distribution center considering 3 sites: Southern California, Mexico, Guatemala
Five years ago, Down Under relocated many manufacturing facilities to South Asia from Australia, boosting long-term profitability
FY 2014 costs are approximately the same as FY 2013 costs

framework: Understand the client: industry, products, channels, customers, competitive position
Diagnose the revenue gap: compare forecast vs. actual sales by channel and category to isolate the shortfall
Diagnose the cost side: compare forecast vs. actual costs to rule out cost overruns
Identify root cause: pinpoint which specific product/channel combination caused the miss
Brainstorm solutions: propose ways to close the gap (channel strategy, product strategy, marketing)
Deliver recommendation: summarize findings, propose next steps, flag risks

questions.prompt: Step 1 — Calculate expected profit from Exhibit 1. What is the earnings shortfall?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare 2014 forecast sales ($12,800M) minus forecast costs ($11,700M) = expected profit $1,100M. Actual sales ($12,000M) minus actual costs ($11,500M) = actual profit $500M. Shortfall = $600M. Revenue miss = $800M; cost savings partially offset.

math.setup: Expected Profit = Forecast Sales - Forecast Costs; Actual Profit = Actual Sales - Actual Costs; Shortfall = Expected - Actual
math.answer: Earnings shortfall = $600M; revenue missed by $800M while costs came in $200M better than forecast

questions.prompt: Step 2 — Using Exhibits 2 and 3, identify which category and channel drove the revenue shortfall.
questions.guidance: Candidate should notice Surf Equipment is a new 2014 category not present in 2012-2013 actuals. Interviewer reveals: Surf Equipment sold $800M at Surf Shops. Forecast was $1,600M at Surf Shops. That is a $800M miss, fully explaining the revenue gap. Candidate should calculate actual units sold: $800M / $400 per unit = 2M units vs. 4M units projected — only 50% of forecasted units sold.

math.setup: Actual Surf Equipment Surf Shop units = Actual Surf Shop Surf Equipment revenue / Average price
steps: Actual Surf Equipment revenue at Surf Shops = $800M (provided by interviewer when prompted)
Forecast units at Surf Shops = 4M (from Exhibit 2)
math.answer: Down Under sold only 2M units of Surf Equipment at Surf Shops vs. 4M forecasted, creating an $800M revenue shortfall that fully explains the earnings miss

questions.prompt: Step 3 — Using Exhibit 4, confirm whether costs are the primary issue.
questions.guidance: Costs are approximately in line with FY 2013 and close to forecast. Surf Equipment has higher marketing costs as a percentage of overall costs due to the recent product launch, but this is already reflected. The cost side is not the primary driver of the miss; the revenue shortfall is.

brainstorming.prompt: Thinking about a customer's shopping experience at a Surf Shop, how could Down Under increase Surf Equipment sales?

categories.name: In-Store Experience
ideas: Dedicated product display or demo zone for surf equipment
Staff training / product knowledge sessions so shop employees can sell the equipment

categories.name: Channel & Distribution
ideas: Expand Surf Equipment into Big Box retail to reach more customers
Explore online direct-to-consumer for Surf Equipment sales
Offer Surf Shops exclusive product configurations to incentivize stocking

categories.name: Marketing & Awareness
ideas: Increase targeted advertising to surfer community
Leverage athlete sponsorships to showcase Surf Equipment
Partner with surf events and competitions for brand visibility
Social media campaigns targeting surfer lifestyle segments

categories.name: Pricing & Promotions
ideas: Introductory pricing or bundle deals (equipment + apparel)
Consignment or return policy to reduce risk for Surf Shop retailers
Loyalty or referral programs for repeat customers

categories.name: Product & Brand
ideas: Ensure product quality and performance credentials are communicated clearly
Address any awareness gap — surfers may not know Down Under now sells equipment
Consider whether product specs match what surfers actually need

recommendation: Down Under missed its 2014 earnings forecast primarily due to lower-than-expected sales of Surf Equipment at Surf Shops — the company sold only 2 million units vs. 4 million projected, creating an $800M revenue shortfall
The new product launch into a tangential category (hard goods/surf equipment) proved challenging; costs were not the main issue as they came in slightly better than forecast
risks: Movement away from core competency (apparel) into hard goods may dilute brand perception
Surf Shops have limited floor space and may be reluctant to carry bulky surf equipment
Lack of channel and consumer awareness of the new product category
Long-term brand impact if equipment quality does not meet the expectations set by the premium apparel brand
next_steps: Develop an actionable plan to increase Surf Equipment sell-through at Surf Shops (staff training, demos, POS materials)
Evaluate expanding Surf Equipment into Big Box and online channels to broaden reach
Assess whether pricing and product positioning are aligned with what Surf Shop customers expect
Determine if additional marketing investment is warranted to build awareness of the new category
Review new manufacturing/distribution center site selection (Southern California, Mexico, Guatemala) for cost and supply chain optimization
